title: Expanding the Defender’s Window with Self-defending Infrastructure
summary: Announcing Shirudo, an open-source project we are co-developing to enable systems to defend themselves and extend the defender’s window.
body_markdown:
While hearing about new security flaws and seeing systems go down as a result of emergency upgrades is unsettling, it’s now a part of our everyday life.


We are in the messy middle of a disruptive, but necessary transition where our critical infrastructure is being rebuilt with AI. It will be more capable, reliable, and intelligent than ever, but the upgrade isn’t going to be without challenges.


Three things are happening at once.


First, AI models are getting good at finding security flaws. The


[PHP flaw](https://blog.talosintelligence.com/two-critical-rces-in-php-core/) from earlier this fall and a


[major Java bug](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/politics/ai-security-bug-java.html) just last week were both found by a startup, Calif, using the OpenAI Cyber model.


Second, attackers are getting better and faster at exploiting these flaws with swarms of agents.


With PHP and Java4shell, exploit campaigns were underway within a day of disclosure, if not before.


Third, the agents we’re deploying in our enterprises are a new risk vector. They need to be protected from attackers looking to exploit them, and they need to be prevented from becoming inadvertent adversaries in pursuit of the goals we give them.


These threats are exacerbated by the speed of AI. Bugs and flaws used to unfold over days and weeks. It’s now minutes and hours. The


[Defender’s Window](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/) is shrinking. Permanent fixes to security flaws take time to develop, test, and deploy. We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place.


## **Self-defending infrastructure**


At Cisco, we’re already using frontier AI to


[discover issues in our own products faster](https://blogs.cisco.com/news/from-flashlight-to-floodlight-what-six-months-of-frontier-ai-has-changed-at-cisco?ccid=cc003711&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter) . We are charter members of both OpenAI’s Daybreak Trusted Access for cyber program and Anthropic’s Project Glasswing. In addition, we’ve


developed


distributed security architectures like Hypershield that enforce security policies directly on workloads and network hardware, and we pioneered Hyrbid Mesh Firewalls


. Most recently,


we’ve been innovating ways to shield our own products (e.g. with


[Live Protect](https://blogs.cisco.com/news/shields-up-cisco-live-protect-closes-vulnerability-gap-with-compensating-controls) ) to give customers more time to patch.


What we’ve learned from these efforts is that today’s moment calls for the next evolution in security architecture. We call it self-defending infrastructure. In practice, that comes down to five principles.


- **Security needs to live inside infrastructure.** For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint. You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it. This approach is fundamentally mismatched to AI. If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind.


- **Agents** **are the operators now.** The only way to combat the speed of threats powered by AI is with AI agents of our own. This doesn’t mean replacing security teams. Self-defending infrastructure gives teams leverage to make it a fair fight.


- **We need to speak the language of agents.** Today’s systems were built for humans. Agents can act directly in code with super human speed and precision. We need tools that enable agents to put defenses right next to the workload and attack path (whether that’s in eBPF in the kernel, Java bytecode, or a firewall or network rule) instead of filtering them through interfaces that were built for people.


- **Continuous learning is the way.** A static policy can’t keep up with adversaries and swarms of agents who adapt in real time. Self-defending agents can monitor false positives, performance, and the health of the service. They can integrate red-team findings and production signals to continuously improve.


- **Trust all the way down.** In security, e


very version of a control needs to be signed and trusted for deployment. This is especially critical as agents begin creating, refining, and deploying defenses.


Proof of where a control came from should travel with it, from the agent that wrote it to the host that runs it.


## **Introducing** **Shirudo**


Self-defending infrastructure requires us to transform many of the building blocks of security.


Today, with OpenAI we are jointly announcing


[Shirudo, an open-source project](https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y2026/m11/cisco-and-openai-launch-shirudo-a-new-project-to-safeguard-agentic-ai.html) we are co-developing to enable systems to defend themselves and address everyone’s first-order problem today, extending the defender’s window.


Shirudo, Japanese for shield, equips security teams with a way to leverage agents to block a path to vulnerable code on a running Linux host while they deploy a permanent fix. It’s built on eBPF, which lets small programs watch or block operations in a running kernel without a restart. Put simply, Shirudo makes eBPF, one of our most important security building blocks, agent-native.


Here’s how it works. Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures. They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it’s safe, and it retires when the real patch lands.


Shirudo’s AI agent-based approach has already written code that detects and blocks attempts to exploit both the recent PHP and Java4shell vulnerabilities. Java4shell could allow attackers to take control of affected servers worldwide, and the PHP vulnerability reportedly affected an estimated 70% of global websites and web infrastructure.


## **What’s next**


You can find deeper dives from our


[Isovalent team](https://isovalent.com/blog/post/cisco-openai-shirudo/) and from[OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/introducing-shirudo/)


on how we’re working together and how Shirudo works. OpenAI brings frontier AI and security and infrastructure research. Our team brings the systems experience, including Isovalent engineers who helped create eBPF. We’ll also explore[Shirudo in detail in our webinar on December 15](https://isovalent.site/4t8Pjxc) .


Shirudo’s runtime is open source. If you’re a kernel developer, an infrastructure operator, a security researcher, or a security vendor, please try it. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability. Run a shield against a kernel build you run. Show us where it breaks legitimate traffic.


We’re only at the beginning of what security and infrastructure builders like Cisco and frontier AI labs like OpenAI can do together. Shirudo is the first of many projects, and we can’t wait to see how the overall effort grows as the community begins to


[build with us](https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo) .
